topic: Parliament sessions, sittings, motions — mixed tiers
description: Budget/Monsoon/Winter sessions, quorum, joint sitting, prorogation, dissolution

questions.stem: The THREE regular sessions of Indian Parliament each year are:

options.option_text: Budget, Monsoon, Winter sessions yearly
Spring, Summer, Autumn sessions yearly
January, May, October sessions yearly
Pre-Budget, Budget, Post-Budget sessions yearly

questions.explanation: Indian Parliament typically has 3 sessions: BUDGET (Jan/Feb to May, longest), MONSOON (July-August/September), WINTER (Nov-Dec). Total ~70-90 sittings per year (declining trend; 1950s used to see ~120). Article 85: gap between two sessions of the same House should not exceed 6 MONTHS. President SUMMONS sessions; PROROGUES (ends) sessions. PARLIAMENT may have a SPECIAL session at any time (e.g., 5-day session Sep 2023 for women's reservation bill).

questions.stem: The QUORUM required for a sitting of either House of Parliament is:

options.option_text: One-fourth of the total membership of the House
One-tenth of the total membership of the House
Half of the total membership of the House
Two-thirds of the total membership of the House

questions.explanation: Article 100(3) — quorum = 1/10 of total membership of a House. Lok Sabha (545 max) → 55. Rajya Sabha (245 max) → 25. If quorum not present, Speaker/Chairman adjourns or suspends sitting. Quorum is NEEDED to conduct any business (debate, vote). For a CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT BILL passage, additional requirements: 2/3 of present + voting, AND majority of total membership.

questions.stem: A JOINT SITTING of the two Houses of Parliament is called under which Article and presided by whom?

options.option_text: Article 108, presided by the Speaker of Lok Sabha
Article 107, presided by the President of India
Article 110, presided by the Vice-President
Article 75, presided by the Prime Minister of India

questions.explanation: Article 108 — JOINT SITTING. Called by President when there's a deadlock between LS and RS on an ordinary bill. Presided by SPEAKER of Lok Sabha (Deputy Speaker if Speaker absent). Decision by simple majority of present + voting. NOT applicable to Money Bills (LS supreme) or Constitutional Amendment Bills (need separate 2/3 in each House). Held only THREE times in Indian history: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Bill (1978), POTA Bill (2002). Article 110 = Money Bill definition. Article 107 = ordinary bills.

questions.stem: Which of these is a MOTION OF NO CONFIDENCE in the government?

options.option_text: Adjournment motion, to discuss an urgent public matter
No-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
Privilege motion, against a member for breach of privilege
Censure motion, against a single minister for misconduct

questions.explanation: NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION — moved in Lok Sabha (not Rajya Sabha). If passed, the Council of Ministers MUST resign (Article 75: cabinet collectively responsible to LS). Needs 50 MPs to support introduction; full debate; voted upon. Government has fallen 4 times via no-confidence: VP Singh (1990), Deve Gowda (1997), Vajpayee (1999, by 1 vote), and the most recent successful one. CENSURE motion — against a specific minister or government for specific policy/action; less serious; doesn't bring down govt. PRIVILEGE motion — against an MP for breach of parliamentary privilege.

questions.stem: The QUESTION HOUR in Parliament is generally held during:

options.option_text: The last hour of the parliamentary working day
The first hour of every parliamentary sitting
Every Friday afternoon, only as a fixed slot
Once a fortnight, on alternate Mondays only

questions.explanation: QUESTION HOUR — first hour of each sitting (11:00 am to 12:00 noon usually) where ministers respond to questions from MPs. Three types of questions: STARRED (oral, marked with asterisk; ministers reply orally; supplementary questions allowed); UNSTARRED (written reply); SHORT NOTICE (urgent matters, less than 10 days notice). ZERO HOUR — the period AFTER Question Hour and BEFORE the agenda begins; informal time for raising urgent issues; an Indian innovation, not in the original Constitution. Very valuable mechanism of executive accountability.

questions.stem: The DIFFERENCE between PROROGATION and DISSOLUTION of a House of Parliament is that:

options.option_text: Both terms mean the same thing in Indian polity
Prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the House's term
Prorogation requires 2/3 majority; dissolution simple majority
Prorogation done by Speaker; dissolution by President

questions.explanation: ADJOURNMENT — short suspension by Speaker/Chairperson within a session; House meets again on the appointed day. PROROGATION — formal end of a session by the President (Article 85); the House CONTINUES to exist (members + Speaker continue in office). DISSOLUTION — Lok Sabha is DISSOLVED by the President; ends the House's term and triggers fresh general elections. Rajya Sabha is a PERMANENT BODY; never dissolved (1/3 retire every 2 years). Distractor 1 — they're different. Distractor 3, 4 wrong specifics.

questions.stem: The presiding officer of the RAJYA SABHA (the Upper House) is the:

options.option_text: Speaker, who also presides over Lok Sabha
Vice-President of India, ex-officio Chairman
President of India, the head of the state
Senior-most member of the House by age only

questions.explanation: Article 64: Vice-President of India is the EX-OFFICIO Chairman of Rajya Sabha. Presides over RS sittings. (NB: VP is NOT a member of RS.) Lok Sabha — has its own Speaker, elected from amongst MPs. DEPUTY CHAIRPERSON of Rajya Sabha — elected from amongst RS members. President doesn't preside over either House (separation of executive + legislature). Distractor 1 — Speaker is for LS only. Distractor 3, 4 wrong.
